newsitem.title: UK: Yeltsin's sacking of Lebed stores up problems.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin's sacking of Lebed stores up problems.

text.p: Commentators across Europe warned on Friday that Russian President Boris Yeltsin's sacking of security chief Alexander Lebed may rebound on the ailing leader and give Lebed a long-term opportunity to reach for power.
Britain's Financial Times, in an editorial headlined "The Battle for Russia" warned: "Few people believe that yesterday's dismissal of Mr Alexander Lebed...marks the end of the story."
And in France, left and right united in their analysis.

The left-leaning daily Liberation said "Boris Yeltsin may be offering the turbulent general an ideal trampoline to succeed him", while the conservative Le Figaro asked: "Has Boris Yeltsin just put Alexander Lebed in orbit?
"By brutally sacking him yesterday for a putsch he didn't commit, he may have opened the way for him towards the next presidential election," Le Figaro added.

Analysts said that although the timing was a shock, Lebed's departure was far from a surprise, "He really did bring this on himself," Margot Light, a lecturer in international relations at the London School of Economics, told Reuters.

Lacking the skills of intrigue needed to negotiate the corridors of power, the blunt-speaking former paratroop general clashed with powerful rivals from the moment Yeltsin brought him into the Kremlin to help him win the July election runoff.
But Lebed, 46, who won the support of 11 million people during the first round of presidential elections in June and enjoys strong backing in the armed forces, has public support.

A recent poll showed Lebed, who on Friday announced plans to stand for president in forthcoming elections, to be Russia's most trusted politician. In London, The Times said Lebed may have been counting on this even before his sacking.
"This could be the best move of Mr Lebed's short political career -- as, by courting dismissal, he seems himself to have calculated," the Times said in an editorial.
"The popular verdict is...likely to be that Mr Lebed was the victim of a Kremlin plot redolent of the Communist era.
"If people conclude that he was duped by Mr Lebed's political enemies, Mr Yeltsin's show of strength may yet come to be seen as further evidence of his weakness."

Denmark's Berlingske Tidende echoed the same theme. "Lebed is Russia's most popular politician and he can now address himself directly to the electorate with a campaign directed against Moscow and the clique that showed him the door."
"Such a strategy has great potential in a Russia where the power-elite is seen, at best, as incapable of solving the country's problems and at worst as corrupt and close-knit.
"One thing only is certain, we have not yet seen the last of the great Russian drama."
The question taxing Russia-watchers now is whether Yeltsin can survive his forthcoming heart surgery, or whether Russia will be plunged into a new presidential election.
With time to build a political network he has so far lacked, Lebed "could be unstoppable in the future", Light said.
"If an election takes place quite soon it will rebound to Lebed's advantage," she said.
But if Yeltsin managed to hold on to power after his surgery in November, Lebed's chances could diminish.
"In the long term it will rebound against Lebed because he doesn't have a stage on which to act, and he does like to portray himself as a man of action," she said.
But as Lebed prepares for his future, analysts are also worried about the possibility of unrest in the armed forces and the effect of his departure on Russia's peace deal in Chechnya.

On Chechnya, the head of an international mediating mission there said on Friday Lebed's sacking as security advisor should not affect the peace process. Russia on Friday said Lebed would continue in his role as chief peace negotiator in Chechnya.
British officials said privately that the general view seemed to be that any organised military turmoil was unlikely. Lebed himself called on his supporters on Thursday to stay calm.

But, citing a letter from a group of General Staff officers in which they told the Defence Ministry to pay all salary arrears by October 25 or face the consequences, he did warn: "We are heading for a very hot autumn, no doubt about it."
